newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak's sons complain about newspaper ad.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak's sons complain about newspaper ad.

text.p: The businessmen sons of Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak have complained to the public prosecutor's office about an advertisement last week in an Arab newspaper, the prosecutor's office said on Tuesday.

The newspaper, Saudi-owned Asharq al-Awsat, could face criminal libel charges for the allegations of corruption and monopolistic practices which appeared in the advertisement, part of a publicity campaign for its magazine al-Jadida.

In a highly unusual move apparently designed to head off speculation among Egyptians about the content of the allegations, Egyptian government newspapers published full details of them on their front pages on Tuesday.
President Mubarak has himself denied rumours that his sons Gamal and Alaa have benefited from their family connections in their business dealings.

Gamal, a former merchant banker with Bank of America, is executive director of the London-based company MedInvest Associates. Alaa, his elder brother, has diverse business interests, mainly inside Egypt.

Gamal has a high public profile as a member of the U.S.-Egyptian Presidents' Council, a private-sector lobbying group which is under a cloud because of a widespread feeling that it was beginning to dictate Egypt's economic policy.
The government newspapers said that the two sons had given evidence in person to the public prosecutor's department as part of the investigations into their complaint.

At this stage it is not clear if the investigations will lead to criminal charges against Asharq al-Awsat. Under Egyptian law, libel and defamation can be criminal offences, in which case it is the prosecutor who decides whether to press charges.
The publishers of the newspaper, London-based Saudi Research and Marketing, released the magazine al-Jadida last week but without the contentious article, a source at the newspaper said.
Officials at the newspaper were unavailable for comment.
The government newspapers said the complaint by the two Mubaraks described the allegations as "pure fabrication with no basis in fact, either as a whole or in detail".
"This amounts to libel and defamation and sullies the reputation of their family," they added, quoting a senior judicial source.
